https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: The shuttered Saudi embassy in Yemen’s capital Sana’a, with a mural depicting a Houthi fighter stopping a ship. Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPA View image in fullscreen The shuttered Saudi embassy in Yemen’s capital Sana’a, with a mural depicting a Houthi fighter stopping a ship. Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPA Yemen Houthis claim attack on Saudi base as fighting flares with Yemeni forces Iran-allied Houthis say drones and missiles used in attack that targeted ‘weapons depots and command and control centres’ in southern Saudi Arabia Agence France-Presse Sat 12 Sep 2026 21.27 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Houthi fighters on Sunday said they used drones and missiles to attack a military base in southern Saudi Arabia as renewed fighting with Yemen’s government forces led growing numbers of civilians to flee . The attack at the southern Sharurah base targeted “weapons depots and command and control centres that are managing the aggression against our nation and people”, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree wrote on X. The date of the operation was not specified. Clashes have increased this week between the Iran-allied Houthis and Yemeni government forces, which are backed by Riyadh. On Saturday, the government forces said they had struck Houthi fighters in the Red Sea city of Mocha, and later attacked other Houthi positions in the south-western part of the country. “Air Force of the Armed Forces targeted positions and barracks of the terrorist Houthi group with three airstrikes” in the Taiz region, the Yemeni military said Sunday in a post on X. The rapid Houthi advance in Yemen: why it matters and what’s at stake Read more The US news site Axios also reported that Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman twice called Donald Trump to request strikes on the Houthis last week, but that the request was rejected. The ongoing clashes follow a week-long Houthi offensive that culminated in the group capturing the remainder of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and several strategic islands, cementing their hold on the Bab al-Mandab strait at the sea’s southern entrance. The waterway has become an important artery for Saudi Arabian oil exports after Iran largely cut off shipments through the Gulf with its blockade on the strait of Hormuz at the start of the Middle East war. The Houthis have recently declared their own maritime blockade of Riyadh’s Red Sea ports. The government news agency Saba reported on Saturday that Yemeni “forces destroyed vehicles and weapons and killed members of the Houthi terrorist militia” near the port of Mocha, and quoted a spokesperson for the forces as saying they had also struck Houthi targets just outside the city. The Houthis, meanwhile, said on Saturday evening that over the past 48 hours, “Saudi enemy aircraft conducted 129 airstrikes” on areas under their control. Yemen’s civil war, which began in 2014 with the Houthi capture of the capital Sana’a, had been dormant since a ceasefire in 2022 but roared back to life in July. Saudi Arabia first entered the war on the side of Yemen’s internationally recognised government in 2015 and continues to support the Aden-based administration. On Saturday night, Saudi authorities said a Houthi projectile fell in an area near the border, hours after issuing alerts warning of the risk of possible attacks. The civil defence directorate said the incident resulted “in two injuries and material damage to a mosque, several buildings, and vehicles”. The Yemeni civil war has uprooted millions of people, and the latest fighting has led even more to flee their homes. The fall of Mocha to the Houthis on Thursday drove many residents to Aden, where the internationally recognised Yemeni government is based. The UN’s migration agency said on Saturday that 76,000 people had fled the fighting since July, a figure that had quadrupled since last week. About 1,400 people had fled to Djibouti, the country’s minister of economy and finance Ilyas Moussa Dawaleh said on Saturday. The renewed fighting in Yemen has killed more than 500 people, according to sources on both sides. Trump on Saturday acknowledged speaking to the de facto Saudi leader but said the Houthis had also “called us and they don’t want to fight with us”. He did not elaborate on whether Washington would take any action, but told reporters that “everything’s gonna work out fine and dandy” in the region. In 2025, the US conducted a seven-week bombing campaign against the Houthis in response to their repeated attacks on Red Sea shipping in support of Hamas in the Gaza war. That ended with a negotiated ceasefire, though the Houthis kept up their missile and drone attacks targeting Israel. More recently, the group has resumed attacks on ships in the Red Sea after declaring their maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia. In Yemen’s capital Sana’a, Houthi supporters celebrated the freeing of 210 prisoners held in areas that fell to the group and had spent up to eight years in jail. https://www.pcmag.com/news/hacker-linked.text:
In September, the infamous ShinyHunters hacking group claimed it had infiltrated the FBI job recruitment portal, stealing confidential data from 5,000 employees and even replacing the FBI logo with its own. The group has been implicated in hacking numerous large, high-profile organizations over the years, from the European Commission to Grand Theft Auto maker Rockstar Games and the software firm behind Canvas.

Now, Reuters reports that a suspected leader of the group, a teenager named Saif al-Din Khader, is being detained in Jordan. Al-Din Khader—who uses the name Rey online—is said to be cooperating with the authorities, helping the FBI and global law enforcement to find the other hackers in the group, according to sources who spoke to Reuters.

According to independent security researcher Brian Krebs, Rey is responsible for releasing a ransomware strain known as ShinySp1d3r and was the administrator of the data leak website for Hellcat, a ransomware group linked to attacks on Schneider Electric, Telefonica, and Orange Romania.

You May Also Like

The FBI has yet to officially confirm the reports. Last month, FBI Director Kash Patel claimed another member of the group had been detained in the Netherlands, who Krebs says is named Pepijn van der Stap. Meanwhile, earlier this week, Reuters reported that ShinyHunters' dark web site had disappeared. Patel said on X earlier this week that the FBI's teams are working on new leads and that more arrests "are on the table."

ShinyHunters says it doesn't plan to ransom the stolen data and that it is not an act of extortion, claiming the attack "was all a marketing campaign to protect our business and actively combat disinformation." The group instead demanded that the FBI remove a public advisory it issued about the group in May 2026, which said the hackers often exaggerated their claims of access to victims' data.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: A fire burns following clashes between police and protesters in front of Milan’s cathedral on Saturday. Photograph: Stefano Porta/LaPresse/AP View image in fullscreen A fire burns following clashes between police and protesters in front of Milan’s cathedral on Saturday. Photograph: Stefano Porta/LaPresse/AP Italy Milan braces for more unrest as debate intensifies over Italy’s ‘lost generation’ Protests and fringe violence expose sharp divide between marginalised and immigrant youth and those with greater prospects Angela Giuffrida in Milan Fri 23 Oct 2026 01.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google M artina Miccichè was filming riot police kicking and beating a teenager with batons as they dragged him along Piazza del Duomo, the central Milan square hosting its cathedral, when she was struck by a flying object, causing a deep gash and bruising near her right eye. The journalist had joined hundreds of mostly young people marching through the northern Italian city on Saturday afternoon to protest over soaring living costs and unaffordable housing, echoing the wider wave of economic discontent fuelling protests across Europe . It wasn’t the first time Italy’s youth have loudly aired their grievances during Giorgia Meloni’s four years as prime minister, despite the risk of falling foul of her ruling coalition’s ever-expanding crackdown on security and public dissent. On Saturday afternoon they plan to protest again in Milan and other major Italian cities. View image in fullscreen Youth protesters clash with police in Piazza del Duomo on Sunday, the second day of unrest in Milan. Photograph: Alessandro Bremec/NurPhoto/Shutterstock Miccichè said the atmosphere last Saturday was peaceful until about 5pm, when police blocked access to Via Broletto, a street about a 10-minute walk away from Piazza del Duomo. “People were angry because they were being repressed,” she said, claiming the police turned “suddenly violent” as they pushed the crowd back with their shields. “The violence escalated. They started to grab people at random, hitting and kicking them. It was shocking.” As the clashes continued and police filled the square with teargas while astonished tourists looked on, a group of masked youths on the fringes headed to the surrounding fashion district, tearing down road signs, setting bins alight and smashing shop windows – among them Footlocker and Levi’s – then looting them. View image in fullscreen Fires were lit in Piazza del Duomo on Saturday during the looting and vandalism. Photograph: Stefano Porta/LaPresse/Shutterstock The vandalism resumed on Sunday as the gangs – many baited by the promise of luxury goods through a network of social media chats – descended on the city centre again, mostly from marginalised areas on the outskirts. During the two days of unrest, police detained more than 271 young people. Of those, 32 were arrested, including 23 minors and 13 foreign nationals. As the Italian media published images of injured police officers, Meloni’s government rapidly enacted more measures targeting minors and further empowering the police – including holding parents financially accountable for their children’s vandalism and looting – while dispatching 500 troops to Milan. View image in fullscreen Clashes with police continued on Sunday in a second day of unrest in Milan. Photograph: Alessandro Bremec/NurPhoto/Shutterstock The latest legislation also criminalises violent participation in ⁠a demonstration and toughens penalties for ⁠rioters. Some of the government’s security measures are now being applied in the south of Italy , where lorry drivers have been protesting against high petrol prices for more than a week, blocking roads and disrupting supermarket supplies. In response, 71 people have been reported to judicial authorities and 242 fined over the blockades – a protest act made illegal in a previous security bill. A government official also warned the lorry drivers that obstructing public highways could carry jail terms. View image in fullscreen Truck drivers blocked streets and tram tracks near the port of Naples on Thursday during a protest against increased fuel costs that began on 16 October. Photograph: Eliano Imperato/AFP/Getty Images “This government just tries to repress protesters instead of listening to them and addressing the issues,” said Miccichè, who needed stitches for her injury. “It is all connected. There is anger in the south over fuel prices and young people everywhere are angry – they don’t even have a chance to think about the future because they are so terrified of the present.” Furthermore, “we are not feeling safe”, the 34-year-old added, “because we can see how much space the police have now and how shielded they are”. Racial profiling had become the norm in Milan, especially in the centre and close to its train stations, she claimed. View image in fullscreen Young demonstrators faced teargas and water cannon in Turin on Saturday. Photograph: Daniele Solavaggione/LaPresse/Shutterstock The weekend’s urban unrest, including protests in Turin and Bologna, has intensified debate over Italy’s “lost generation”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Furthermore, the youth protests and subsequent fringe violence have exposed the sharp divide between Italy’s marginalised and immigrant youth and those with greater prospects. Working-class Italians or third- and second-generation immigrants are regularly labelled by rightwing politicians and the press as maranza , a derogatory term used to describe groups of young people who usually congregate in city centres. They come from areas like Barona, a sprawling council estate in the south-west of Milan. Young people there have been reflecting on the events of last weekend. “There is a lot of discontent – we are all children of this widespread malaise,” said Domenico Ricci, who along with Luca Orlando manages a bar that is part of Barrio’s , a cultural hub where the district’s youth come together. View image in fullscreen Protesters clash with police in Piazza del Duomo, Milan, on Sunday. Photograph: Alessandro Bremec/NurPhoto/Shutterstock Orlando believes the vandalism and looting were a symptom of anger and years of feeling unheard and invisible. “So when an opportunity arises, these kids take revenge. They don’t do it simply because they want to steal something. All this government does is introduce new crimes – they never listen or engage in dialogue.” Orlando, whose parents came from Calabria, is feeling the nationwide discontent. “But the protests there [in the south-west] have hardly had any coverage,” he said. “And we are only talking about Milan because of the violence and not the real issues.” Thomas, 18, who has grown up in Barona, is training to be a chef and wants to leave Italy “as soon as possible”. He said: “I see no future here.” His friend Mohamed, an Italian citizen of Moroccan origin, is still at high school and wants to become a lawyer. “If you make a mistake, then you must pay,” he said. “But this is also a characteristic of protests – the more a government doesn’t listen, the more people get angry.” Mauro Magatti, a sociologist at Milan’s Catholic University of the Sacred Heart, said socioeconomic discomfort and a sense of abandonment affected “an entire generation” and responding to the anger with excessive repression risked enlarging the protest. “Violence always needs to be condemned but now we need to lower the tone to overcome this burst of anger and violence and focus on addressing the real problems,” he said. View image in fullscreen Rightwing demonstrators held a ‘zero tolerance’ protest in Milan on Wednesday as law enforcement stepped up its presence. Photograph: Andrea Carrubba/Anadolu/Getty Images Police and military presence in central Milan has been building in recent days before Saturday’s protest, organised by a new online movement which has pledged to gather each weekend “until this government of thieves falls”. Security guards stood outside shops that had been damaged or looted last weekend. Italy’s politicians from across the spectrum must take heed, warned Miccichè, as the protests were only set to amplify ahead of general elections next year. “There is no perception at all of how young people feel,” she said. “Even if they took just a minute to listen, they will understand that it is a generation full of ideas – they just want to be heard.” Explore more on these topics Italy Protest Cost of living crisis Activism Europe news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Macron bans ‘illegitimate’ protests in France as he tries to get a grip on unrest Angry lawyers and bewildered defendants: the fallout from fast-tracking French rioting cases Europe’s far right seizes on protest violence to push authoritarian anti-immigration agenda Macron accuses Trump and other foreign leaders of ‘stupid comments’ about France unrest Why are French police so violent? https://www.chronicle.lu/category/intern.text: Home News International News Poland's Sikorski Calls for Rapid Ceasefire in Black Sea to Allow Food Shipments Poland's Sikorski Calls for Rapid Ceasefire in Black Sea to Allow Food Shipments Published on Saturday, 31 Oct 2026 09:37 by EO Share This Article: Rate this item: Poland's Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski attends the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Atlanta, Georgia, US, on 30 October 2026; Credit: REUTERS/Megan Varner/Pool ATLANTA (Reuters) - Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski on Friday 30 October 2026 called for a rapid ceasefire in the Black Sea that would allow safe passage for grain shipments from both Ukraine and Russia and said Moscow must end its war against Ukraine before being allowed to resume energy sales to Europe. " I spoke in favour of doing something quickly because the people of the Global South need this grain ," Sikorski told reporters during a two-day meeting of foreign ministers from the Group of 20 major economies in Atlanta. Sikorski, invited to attend the meeting by the US host nation, said that Ukraine must be included in any effort to end Russia's invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year. Europe also had " cards " in the issue and should be involved, he said. He also called for a " fair end " to the war in Ukraine before Russia was able to sell its energy products once again to Europe, formerly its most lucrative market. The United States (US), which holds the rotating presidency of the G20 this year, has proposed that Poland become a full member, much like Germany or France, which are also represented through the European Union (EU). Sikorski said he welcomed the push and had discussed it with a number of G20 member countries in bilateral meetings in Atlanta. Western officials say it could take years for Poland to be accepted as a full member given Russia's opposition and the G20's requirement for consensual decisions. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov told reporters that inviting Poland to attend G20 meetings was counterproductive and broke with diplomatic practice of seeking consensus at such gatherings, according to Russian news agencies. " Of course, this violates the principles of diplomacy, and especially multilateral diplomacy, when members of associations such as the G20 work on the basis of consensus ," Lavrov was quoted as saying. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking at a reception for the ministers at Atlanta's Georgia Aquarium, said Poland deserved to be made a full member. " President (Donald) Trump believes their economic success and growing global influence is exactly what the G20 needs to tackle the major economic challenges we all face ," Rubio said. Sikorski told reporters that Britain, which will head the G20 next year, had already invited Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk to attend the 2027 leaders summit in Manchester, England. https://nassauweekly.com/at-the-end-of-t.text: Nassau Weekly At the End of the Pasture The young boy watched flakes of paint molt off the doorframe as his father’s feet slipped on the dust-covered floor, and his pregnant mother screamed. Mr. Klement had taken a week between harvests last year to coat every doorway in their home with white lead paint, but they had all begun peeling. The boy crunched a flake between his fingers, letting the miniscule pieces flutter to the ground. Beyond the threshold, his mother gripped her stomach as she lay sprawled across his parents’ bed, her knuckles turning the same powder color as the paint. Mr. Klement had told Eddie that she was not going to suffer, that his little sibling would arrive just as easily as he had. Eddie turned away from his mother’s voice, which was once more yelling for her husband. A cow mooed in the distance. Its high-pitched voice lured Eddie to the window. The new calf was his favorite, as it was the first he had ever helped his father deliver. He stood on the tips of his toes to try and spot the little animal in the twilight. His younger sister’s footsteps fell heavily on the staircase behind him. Brown-tinted water sloshed around in the ceramic pot in Mary’s hands. An intricate pink-carnation pattern looped around its rim. Eddie squeezed his eyes shut and shielded them with his hands as his mother’s screaming rattled the windowpanes, shaking dust and spiders from the deepest crevices of the wall. “Eddie!” Mr. Klement shouted at his only son. The boy opened his eyes to see his father knelt down in front of him. “Eddie, listen to me. Can you do a grown-up job for me?” The ten-year-old nodded. “I need you to drive my truck fast to the DeMunds’ house, and I need you to knock on the door until someone answers, okay?” Another nod. Sweat rolled down the man’s face in thick bullets, blending with the tears starting to well on his lower eyelids. His murky eyes darted left and right, left and right, as they searched his son’s face for any sign of confidence. “When someone opens the door, I want you to tell them that the baby’s coming, your mom ain’t too well, she’s bleeding to death, and you need to use their telephone to call a doctor, okay?” Eddie nodded again. His father gritted his teeth before grabbing the boy’s shoulders and shaking him. Eddie’s neck jerked backwards, and pieces of paint fell from his hands. “God-damn-it, boy,” Mr. Klement said, not removing his hands as he enunciated each word. “Tell me you can do it!” “I can! I can!” Eddie cried. “What are you going to tell them?” “That mama and the baby need a doctor!” Mr. Klement flung his son toward the staircase before standing. He resumed his position by his wife’s side as Mary dabbed her mother’s head with a wet rag. Alone in the hallway, the boy’s wool hole-ridden socks remained nailed to the hardwood floors. He had never dialed a telephone before. “Get your ass out of here, boy!” Eddie broke into a sprint, his feet barely touching every third step of the ancient staircase. Grandma Schovajsa’s old persian rug slipped beneath him, causing him to stumble out the screen door and trip off the front porch. He regained his footing and stared out to the miles of dusty farmland. Cattle loitered under the treeline at the far end of the pasture. The new calf mooed as it was licked clean by its mother, a half-ton cow Mrs. Klement had named Shirley. In the distance, their barn broke the fluidity of the horizon, now backlit by the setting sun. No other buildings were in sight; the DeMund’s wood-frame house sat more than a mile down the dirt and pebble road. The truck’s wooden runners creaked and groaned under Eddie’s weight as he lifted himself onto the bench seat. A field mouse scurried out from underneath him. His eyes—usually five feet from the ground—struggled to see over the dashboard and out the windshield. Eddie turned the coil switch as he had watched Mr. Klement do a thousand times before. To start the truck, he needed to push down on the starting switch, which was mounted to the floor, beyond the reach of his foot. He slid down the bench until he rested on the small of his back, and his head was level with the dashboard. The engine sputtered to life and began puttering in sync with the rattle of the hood. The boy mimicked his father as well as his young memory could allow: down went the pedal farthest from the steering column, towards him went the gear stick to his right. The thin wooden-spoke wheels rolled as if they were turtles waking from a deep nap; the countryside almost stayed still beyond the windows. Eddie maneuvered the old beast onto Schovajsa Road, named after his mother’s invariable Czech family. The truck’s chassis jolted with each stone in the truck’s path, lurching Eddie around behind the wheel. Eddie cautiously changed into second gear as the truck propelled pebbles behind it. The DeMunds were their nearest—and only—neighbors. For six decades, Albert and Irene DeMund had farmed the same plot of land with a rotation of sons, daughters, and laborers. Eddie had spent uncountable hours in their single-story house that looked out onto where Schovajsa Road turned into Main Street. Five agonizing minutes later, the truck arrived next to the DeMunds’ rusting mailbox. Eddie flung the door open, dashing to the house without turning off the car. “Help! Help!” He screamed as he ran up the path, waving his arms above his head. Through the windows, the curtain glowed with soft orange candle light, untouched by any shadows. Pain shot up his legs as his socked feet fell prey to sharp rocks and twigs in the front yard. He had vague recollections of green grass and rain blanketing their land, but he could not imagine it now. Stones pierced his socks like thorns until he found himself on the DeMund’s doorstep. He pounded on the door with his knuckles, then the balls of his fists. A floorboard creaked and an old woman pulled the door open. “Edd—” “The baby’s comin’. Daddy says mama’s bleedin’ to death. And I’ve gotta use your phone!” The boy barely had time to catch his breath before Mrs. DeMund was in the living room, receiver to her ear and mouthpiece in front of her face. She asked the operator to call Dr. Andersson, who held the only medical degree in a 20 mile radius. “Doctor?” “It’s Irene DeMund.” “Yes, I’m fine. Heddy Klement needs you as soon as possible.” As Mrs. DeMund gave the doctor directions to the Klements’ house, Eddie stood frozen in their entryway. Mr. Klement had helped build the DeMunds’ home, and Mrs. Klement, not yet a mother, had labored alongside her husband for days. A testament to their town’s community, the DeMunds allowed the 12 people who had pitched in to carve their initials on a random plank, which was eventually used for the entryway’s floor. Eddie stared at his mother’s initials which, unlike the others, were not suffocated by a thick rug. Mr. DeMund emerged from their bedroom and approached Eddie. He patted the boy’s disheveled hair with his calloused hands. “Whatcha doing here so late, son?” He asked. He peaked around the corner to greet Eddie’s parents only to find his wife setting down their telephone. Before Eddie could repeat his father’s message, Mrs. DeMund came out of the living room and whispered instructions into her husband’s ear. “I’ll drive us all back—” “Albert, he can’t see her like this again.” Mrs. DeMund took Eddie’s hands in hers. “You stay here with Al, okay? Your mother will be just alright. The doctor’s on his way—he just needs to check up on things.” Eddie nodded in response. Mrs. DeMund’s eyes lacked their usual glow. He watched as she kissed his forehead then disappeared out the front door. The Chevy’s engine sputtered to a start, but was replaced by the sound of cicadas and rustling cornstalks as she drove further down the road. The tiny room fell silent. Mr. DeMund had changed out of his work clothes, now donning worn brown slacks and a fresh cotton shirt. His big toe protruded from his left sock, while his other foot was still protected by a leather boot. “Why don’t we go into the kitchen and eat?” Mr. DeMund asked as he acclimated to the task his wife had assigned him. Had he opened the door for Eddie, he would have driven all three of them back to the Klements’ house. In the years that followed, Eddie would wish that that would have been the case. The old man continued. “Have you eaten yet, son?” “No, sir. The baby started coming while mama was cooking,” Eddie explained. “It’s coming early.” “What was she making?” “Meatloaf and griddle cakes.” Mr. DeMund chuckled despite himself. “Your mother is a good cook. I bet your little sibling just smelled her food on the stove and wanted a piece of it.” “Yessir,” Eddie said fast enough that the syllables blended into one, polite noise. Mr. DeMund turned and began walking to the kitchen. Eddie followed. Their kitchen impressed him, even at his young age—cupboards covered in enamel tile, a farmhouse sink, and a yellow range stove filled the room. Mrs. DeMund had covered walls with the same floral pattern that she had painted on Mrs. Klement’s pot, but in her signature yellow. Eddie counted the carnations around the molding as Mr. DeMund surveyed the cupboards. His hands shook imperceptibly. Eddie watched as the old man crafted his sandwich, taking care to align the cheese and butter in the middle of the sliced bread. He presented the creation to the boy on a porcelain plate with a glass of foaming, lukewarm milk and two pieces of taffy. “Michael brought them from Omaha the last time he visited,” he said, motioning toward the sticky delicacies. “Said they’re world-famous.” Eddie had seen the exact candy in the town’s general store several days before. The 17-year-old behind the counter, a malnourished farm boy by the name of Glenn, had a tendency of sneaking a handful from the jar during his shifts. The two moved to the dining room, where Eddie alternated between bites of sandwich and tepid sips of milk. Mr. DeMund sat opposite of him. His arms were four shades darker than his face, the result of decades out in the corn fields. He leaned his elbows on the table and clasped his hands in front of his beard. Mementos of a life well-lived surrounded them: sepia photographs of their large family on the walls, a bureau displaying seldom-used wedding china, and damask curtains from their second son, George, who had escaped to the East Coast. Mrs. Klement had taught her son to never ask questions about money. People either had money or didn’t; there was no use in making them articulate which category they fell into. So, Eddie finished his sandwich in silence. He ate at a snail’s pace as he waited for the sound of their truck and Mrs. DeMund with good news. Instead, the cicadas’ shrill song filled the night with an antagonizing hum. Eddie cleaned his dishes himself. At ten, he was already tall enough to reach over their gaping sink without being lifted. His mother sometimes teased him for this fact of life, calling him her “obr,” or giant. “Why don’t we call it a night?” Mr. DeMund said, more as a command rather than a question. “I’m sure there will be news in the morning. You’ll want to get a good night’s rest before you start playing with your new sibling.” Eddie obliged with a sunken heart. He fiddled with his hands, cracking his knuckles and repeatedly clasping them. No other farm families in the area had just two children, but no other farming families had his mother’s misfortune. He could picture her all alone in her bed, another year with another empty bassinet. As they walked to the spare bedroom, a dim light passed the transom window above the front door. It grew brighter as the groan of the doctor’s Studebaker traversed the uneven dirt road. Eddie ran and broke through the door within seconds. In the faint moonlight, he saw Dr. Andersson squint at the address on the mailbox, shake his head, and continue down the road. Eddie sprinted after the car. He shouted for the doctor to stop over the onslaught of noise until his throat burned. Thirty feet down the road, the gleaming car came to a halt. Without hesitation, Eddie hopped onto the running board and gripped the passenger-side door. He could see Mr. DeMund on his front porch over his shoulder. “I need to see my mom,” Eddie cried over the door. “I need to hold her hand.” Dr. Andersson opened the door from the inside. Eddie mumbled a thank you as he slid in. He had seen Dr. Andersson once, in the general store in front of the taffy jar. The five minute journey felt like 20 as the boy watched the monotonous scenery pass them by. Corn and insufficient hedgerows melted into one behind his tears, until he could not tell how much distance they had already covered. “Your mother is a strong woman,” Dr. Andersson said as they passed a lone deer. Eddie could not remember his mother ever meeting the doctor. The Klements’ white-wood house appeared over the horizon like Goliath coming to defeat David. At the first sight of it, Eddie sprang from his seat and leaped from the moving car. The pain in his feet disappeared as he ran through the only world that he had ever known. A flock of birds circled overhead and disrupted the cloudless sky—Eddie did not waste the time to look up and see that they were crows. Eddie pushed open their front door, rotting and in need of replacement, with ease. Inside, everything was the same: the matted rug was slightly askew, wilted flowers graced the table in the hall, and his wooden train was parked around the corner. In Eddie’s lifetime, he could not remember their home being as clean and well-decorated as the DeMunds’, even before the dust had taken its toll. But every woodpecker’s hole on the outside of their house was ingrained into his memory, and every creaky floorboard was mapped out in his head. With one hand on the rail, Eddie crept up the stairs into the suffocating silence. No photographs of family covered the adjacent wall; rather, the striped wallpaper stood bare against the elements. At the top of the stairs, the ceramic pot was discarded on the bench where he had first learned to read. A plume of dust lifted off the landing as Eddie turned towards the northern end of the hall. The creak of two doors opening simultaneously split his attention as Mrs. DeMund exited the nursery and Mr. Andersson walked into the home. Eddie examined the woman who his family had placed their faith in. The color had gone from her face hours ago, but she had not started crying, not yet. Her hands were wet, and deep red and brown stains muddled her dress. “Oh, Eduard…” It was all she could say. Even when the doctor asked her for Mrs. Klement, it was all she said to the boy. She wrapped her arms around him as a shield from something he thought he knew all too well as he listened to his father and Mr. Andersson talk in the bedroom. The doctor returned to the hall within minutes, stuffing his golden pocketwatch back into his jacket. His black bag had not been opened, nor his hands bloodied. “Is the baby alive?” His voice dripped with doubt. Mrs. DeMund motioned to the nursery. “In there. A girl.” “Healthy?” “Fit as a fiddle. Mary is with her now.” Mr. Andersson nodded. He turned to the nursery, peering into the room at Eddie’s last piece of his mother. Though the boy did not move, he knew that his mother was not there. Dr. Andersson eyed Mrs. DeMund, whose shoulders had deflated. Her boots lay discarded in the corner, and her stockings made no noise against the floor when she tapped her foot. Eddie noticed that her calves were speckled with bruises and sunspots. With a huff, the old lady knelt down on both knees. Dust clung to her skirt. “Eddie,” she began. Her mouth hung open as she searched for words. “Your mother loves you very much.” “I know that, ma’am.” “When I got here, Mrs. Heddy”—she always called her Mrs. Heddy when talking to Eddie and Mary—“was already asleep.
